human_interventions.name: Cardiorespiratory fitness (elite vs low, observational)
human_interventions.direction: HR is for LOW fitness vs ELITE fitness (i.e. low fitness is 5x deadlier). Inverted protective HR approx 0.20.
human_interventions.population: Adults referred for exercise treadmill testing, Cleveland Clinic 1991-2014, mean age 53, 59% male
human_interventions.evidence_grade: C (large observational, single referred clinical cohort, single fitness measurement; no RCT of fitness on mortality exists)
human_interventions.study: Mandsager et al., JAMA Network Open 2018
human_interventions.harms: None from the exposure itself; the risk is over-interpretation as causal.
human_interventions.note: No upper limit of benefit observed - the dose-response did not plateau at elite fitness. In the SAME cohort, smoking carried HR 1.41 (1.36-1.46) and below-average vs above-average fitness carried HR 1.41 (1.34-1.49); i.e. being unfit was at least as strongly associated with death as smoking.

human_interventions.name: Cardiorespiratory fitness (below-average vs above-average)
human_interventions.direction: HR for below-average vs above-average fitness
human_interventions.evidence_grade: C
human_interventions.study: Mandsager et al., JAMA Network Open 2018
human_interventions.note: Reference comparator within the same cohort.

human_interventions.name: Smoking (within Mandsager cohort, for calibration)
human_interventions.evidence_grade: C (observational within this cohort; smoking causality itself is grade A from other evidence)
human_interventions.study: Mandsager et al., JAMA Network Open 2018
human_interventions.note: Included as an internal yardstick, not as the primary evidence for smoking harm.

human_interventions.name: Leisure-time physical activity, 3-5x the minimum recommendation
human_interventions.population: Pooled prospective cohorts (NCI Cohort Consortium); exact N not surfaced
human_interventions.evidence_grade: C (pooled observational; self-reported exposure)
human_interventions.study: Arem et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 2015
human_interventions.harms: No mortality harm detected at high volumes in this analysis; the benefit plateaued rather than reversed.
human_interventions.note: At 3x the minimum, HR 0.63. The upper threshold of benefit occurred at 3-5x the recommendation (HR 0.61). This is the key dose-response datum against the 'exercise U-curve' claim at recreational volumes. CI not surfaced - must be retrieved.

human_interventions.name: Muscle-strengthening (resistance) activity, 30-60 min/week
human_interventions.endpoint: all-cause mortality (also CVD, total cancer, diabetes, lung cancer)
human_interventions.evidence_grade: C (observational meta-analysis, self-reported exposure)
human_interventions.study: Momma et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine 2022
human_interventions.note: J-shaped dose-response: benefit maximal at 30-60 min/week, with NO conclusive additional benefit beyond ~60 min/week. Independent of aerobic activity. This is a genuine U/J-curve finding, in contrast to aerobic activity (Arem) and CRF (Mandsager) which showed no reversal.

human_interventions.name: Semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly (SELECT)
human_interventions.population: Adults >=45y with overweight/obesity (BMI>=27) and established CVD, WITHOUT diabetes; mean follow-up ~40 months
human_interventions.evidence_grade: B (single large RCT, hard endpoint, but all-cause mortality was a secondary/supportive endpoint not protected by the hierarchical testing sequence; not independently replicated)
human_interventions.study: Lincoff et al., NEJM 2023 (SELECT)
human_interventions.harms: Substantial lean-mass loss (see body-composition entries); GI adverse events; discontinuation rates. Gallbladder disease and pancreatitis signals not verified this session.
human_interventions.note: ARR/NNT NOT COMPUTABLE from retrieved data: the absolute event percentages for all-cause death were not surfaced. Do not quote an ARR without retrieving them. Also: the trial ran through the COVID-19 pandemic peak, and a JACC 2024 analysis found HR 0.84 (0.72-0.98) in participants without COVID and 0.74 (0.55-0.99) in those with COVID (p-interaction 0.46), raising the question of how much of the all-cause signal is infection-related rather than atherosclerotic.

human_interventions.name: Semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly (SELECT)
human_interventions.endpoint: MACE (CV death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke)
human_interventions.evidence_grade: A (prespecified primary endpoint of an adequately powered RCT)
human_interventions.study: Lincoff et al., NEJM 2023 (SELECT)
human_interventions.note: 20% relative risk reduction. RELATIVE-vs-ABSOLUTE CAUTION: the absolute event rates were not surfaced this session, so the ARR and NNT are null. A 20% RRR on a ~8% 40-month event rate corresponds to a low-single-digit ARR; do not let the '20%' stand alone.

human_interventions.name: Semaglutide 2.4 mg (STEP-1 body composition substudy)
human_interventions.evidence_grade: B (RCT substudy, DXA)
human_interventions.study: STEP-1 body-composition substudy
human_interventions.harms: Roughly 40% of total weight lost was lean mass. In an older population this is a plausible sarcopenia/frailty risk that no trial has yet powered a mortality endpoint against.
human_interventions.note: N and CIs not surfaced. The lean-mass fraction figure is the crux of the 'is this a geroprotector or a cardiometabolic drug' question.

human_interventions.name: Tirzepatide (SURMOUNT-1 body composition substudy)
human_interventions.evidence_grade: B (RCT substudy)
human_interventions.study: Look et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2025 (SURMOUNT-1 body composition)
human_interventions.note: CONTRADICTION FLAGGED: the trial substudy suggests tirzepatide preserves lean mass BETTER than semaglutide (25% vs 40% of weight lost), while a 2026 real-world body-composition phenotyping preprint reports tirzepatide causes GREATER lean-mass decline than semaglutide (excess LBM loss 1.1/1.5/1.3/2.0% at 3/6/9/12 months). Trial substudies and routine-care cohorts disagree; neither is dispositive. Report both.

human_interventions.name: RTB101 10 mg daily x 16 weeks (PROTECTOR-1, phase 3)
human_interventions.endpoint: clinically symptomatic respiratory illness in adults >=65
human_interventions.population: Adults >=65, excluding current smokers and COPD
human_interventions.evidence_grade: A (adequately powered phase 3 RCT) - for a NULL result
human_interventions.arr_note: Absolute difference favours placebo by 2 percentage points; not a benefit.
human_interventions.study: resTORbio PROTECTOR-1, announced Nov 2019
human_interventions.note: The single most important negative result in human mTOR-inhibition geroscience. The positive phase 2b (Mannick et al., Sci Transl Med 2018) did not replicate. Development halted. A published post-mortem exists: 'RTB101 and immune function in the elderly: Interpreting an unsuccessful clinical trial'.

human_interventions.name: Everolimus (RAD001) low dose, 6 weeks (Mannick 2014)
human_interventions.endpoint: influenza vaccine antibody response in adults >=65
human_interventions.evidence_grade: C (small phase 2 RCT, immunological SURROGATE endpoint only)
human_interventions.study: Mannick et al., Science Translational Medicine 2014;6(268):268ra179
human_interventions.harms: Dose-dependent adverse events; mouth ulcers/aphthous stomatitis are the classic dose-limiting toxicity. Quantitative AE rates not surfaced.
human_interventions.note: Also reduced the percentage of PD-1-expressing CD4 and CD8 T cells. This is a mechanistic/surrogate result. It was later NOT borne out at the level of clinical infection outcomes in phase 3.

human_interventions.name: Rapamycin 5 or 10 mg weekly, 48 weeks (PEARL)
human_interventions.direction: NULL - primary endpoint not met at either dose
human_interventions.population: Healthy adults 50-85, decentralised trial, compounded rapamycin
human_interventions.evidence_grade: B (RCT, but small, decentralised, surrogate endpoint, and the primary endpoint FAILED)
human_interventions.study: PEARL trial, medRxiv 2024 / published 2025
human_interventions.harms: Reported as relatively safe over 48 weeks at low intermittent doses. No mortality or hard-endpoint data.
human_interventions.note: The widely circulated positive claim is a SECONDARY outcome in a SUBGROUP: lean tissue mass +4.5% over 48 weeks in WOMEN on 10 mg only. That is a sex x dose x outcome selection from a trial whose primary endpoint failed. It is hypothesis-generating, not evidence of a geroprotective effect. Trial was run by a telehealth company that sells rapamycin - an industry-funding consideration.

human_interventions.name: Nicotinamide riboside, 12 weeks, mild cognitive impairment
human_interventions.endpoint: cognitive function (PRIMARY); cerebral blood flow, BP (secondary)
human_interventions.direction: NULL on all endpoints despite ~2-fold increase in blood NAD+
human_interventions.evidence_grade: B (RCT, pilot-scale, null)
human_interventions.study: Randomized placebo-controlled trial of NR in older adults with MCI (2023/2025)
human_interventions.note: TEXTBOOK MECHANISM-OUTCOME DISSOCIATION: the pharmacodynamic target (blood NAD+) was hit decisively (2x) and nothing clinical moved. Raising blood NAD+ is not evidence of benefit.

human_interventions.name: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN)
human_interventions.endpoint: fasting glucose, fasting insulin, HbA1c, insulin resistance, lipid profile
human_interventions.evidence_grade: B (meta-analysis of RCTs, null)
human_interventions.study: Systematic review and meta-analysis of NMN on glucose and lipid metabolism (2024)
human_interventions.note: No significant benefit on any metabolic endpoint pooled across 8 RCTs.

human_interventions.name: NMN / NR on skeletal muscle
human_interventions.endpoint: skeletal muscle index, handgrip strength, gait speed
human_interventions.evidence_grade: B (meta-analysis of RCTs)
human_interventions.study: Prokopidis et al., J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2025; DOI 10.1002/jcsm.13799
human_interventions.note: Effect estimates NOT surfaced before budget exhaustion. FOLLOW-UP REQUIRED. Only the framing ('evidence remains inconclusive') was retrieved.

human_interventions.name: NMN 300/600/900 mg daily, 60 days (Yi 2023)
human_interventions.direction: POSITIVE at 600 and 900 mg; null at 300 mg
human_interventions.evidence_grade: C (short RCT, functional surrogate, sponsor-linked, not independently replicated)
human_interventions.study: Yi et al. 2023, multicentre dose-dependent NMN trial
human_interventions.note: This is the trial most often cited as positive evidence for NMN. It contradicts the null metabolic and muscle meta-analyses. 60-day duration; 6MWT is highly effort- and expectancy-sensitive. The commercial sponsorship of this trial was NOT verified in this session and must be checked before characterising it.

human_interventions.name: Metformin + 12 weeks aerobic exercise training (Konopka 2019)
human_interventions.endpoint: VO2max and whole-body insulin sensitivity gains from training
human_interventions.direction: HARM - metformin ATTENUATED the training-induced increase in both
human_interventions.evidence_grade: B (double-blind RCT, mechanistic/physiological endpoint)
human_interventions.study: Konopka et al., Aging Cell 2019
human_interventions.harms: Blunts the single best-evidenced modifiable mortality predictor (cardiorespiratory fitness).
human_interventions.note: This is the most important practical argument against prophylactic metformin in non-diabetic, exercising adults. Effect sizes not surfaced. Independent of treatment, training still improved fat mass, HbA1c, fasting insulin, 24h glucose and glycaemic variability.

human_interventions.name: Metformin monotherapy vs matched non-diabetic controls (Bannister 2014)
human_interventions.direction: Reported metformin-treated diabetics outliving non-diabetic controls
human_interventions.evidence_grade: D (observational, and specifically REJECTED as evidence of a geroprotective effect - see errors.E1)
human_interventions.study: Bannister et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2014
human_interventions.note: DO NOT USE AS EVIDENCE OF BENEFIT. The adjusted HR was not surfaced; the quoted figures are UNADJUSTED rates. A 2022 Danish cohort failed to replicate, finding HIGHER mortality among metformin users than non-diabetics. See errors.E1.

human_interventions.name: Metformin (TAME trial)
human_interventions.endpoint: composite of major age-related disease events
human_interventions.evidence_grade: U (unknown - trial not completed)
human_interventions.study: TAME (Targeting Aging with Metformin), AFAR / Barzilai
human_interventions.note: As of 2026 the trial has been delayed since 2016 and no efficacy results are published. Sources conflict on whether enrolment has begun: AFAR's own page still describes TAME prospectively (needing funding, participants and a regulatory indication for ageing), while some secondary sources claim enrolment is ongoing. TREAT AS NOT YET RUN. Reportedly now being pursued via ARPA-H.

human_interventions.name: Caloric restriction, 2 years (CALERIE-2)
human_interventions.population: Healthy non-obese adults aged 21-50, 3 US sites
human_interventions.evidence_grade: B for the surrogate; U for mortality (no mortality data exist)
human_interventions.study: Waziry et al., Nature Aging 2023
human_interventions.harms: Bone mineral density loss at lumbar spine, total hip and femoral neck; lean mass loss; reduced muscle strength in older groups (Villareal et al., JBMR 2016).
human_interventions.note: SURROGATE ONLY. The frequently repeated translation of '2-3% DunedinPACE slowing' into '10-15% mortality reduction' is an EXTRAPOLATION from separate observational calibration cohorts, not a measured trial outcome. Also: 1 of several DNAm clocks moved; PhenoAge and GrimAge did not.

human_interventions.name: Low-volume alcohol consumption
human_interventions.direction: NO significant reduction after adjustment for study-design biases
human_interventions.evidence_grade: B (meta-analysis of cohorts with bias adjustment, triangulated with Mendelian randomization)
human_interventions.study: Zhao, Stockwell et al., JAMA Network Open 2023
human_interventions.harms: Alcohol raises blood pressure and stroke risk; MR shows a monotonic, not J-shaped, relationship.
human_interventions.note: The apparent protective effect of moderate drinking disappears when lifetime abstainers are used as the reference and former drinkers are not misclassified as non-drinkers. Corroborated by genetic evidence: Millwood et al., Lancet 2019 (China Kadoorie Biobank, 512,715 enrolled, 161,498 genotyped for ALDH2-rs671 and ADH1B-rs1229984) found no protective effect of moderate intake on stroke and a causal effect on blood pressure. Effect estimates from Millwood not surfaced.

calerie.design: Multicentre RCT, 3 US sites, 2:1 randomisation to 25% caloric restriction vs ad libitum control, 24 months

markers.note: CRITICAL: CALERIE-2 therefore tests ~12% CR, NOT 25% CR. Every downstream claim about '25% caloric restriction in humans' is mis-specified. Sources surfaced '13% energy restriction over 2 years'; the frequently quoted 11.9% two-year average was not independently confirmed this session.
Statistically significant per the primary report; exact p not surfaced. Waziry et al., Nature Aging 2023.
Negative. GrimAge is the clock best calibrated to mortality - its null result is the more mortality-relevant one and is systematically under-reported.
Villareal et al., JBMR 2016. Femoral neck BMD loss is directly on the hip-fracture causal path, a major driver of mortality in the elderly.
Resorption up + formation down = uncoupled remodelling, the unfavourable pattern.
Reduced in young and older adults; muscle strength reduced in older groups. Magnitudes not surfaced.
Kraus et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2019. EXPLORATORY outcomes - explicitly labelled as such in the title.
Hastings et al., Aging Cell 2024 analysed telomere length in CALERIE-2. Result direction NOT retrieved. FOLLOW-UP REQUIRED.
NONE. CALERIE was never powered or long enough for any hard endpoint. There is no human RCT evidence that caloric restriction extends life.

studies.study: University of Wisconsin (Colman et al., Science 2009; Nature Communications 2014)
studies.finding: Significant positive effect of ~30% CR on age-related mortality; the 2014 follow-up reported significant effects on both age-related AND all-cause survival.
No significant survival effect; a trend toward improved health.

studies.study: Joint reconciliation (Mattison et al., Nature Communications 2017)
studies.finding: Collaborative re-analysis by both teams; concluded CR is beneficial in adult and older primates but not when begun in juveniles.

why_they_disagreed.detail: NIA controls were PORTION-fed rather than truly ad libitum and ate less than Wisconsin controls; their lower intake was itself associated with improved survival. The NIA 'control' arm was therefore partially calorie-restricted, biasing toward the null. Wisconsin controls additionally received ~20 g of extra chow per day to eat at will.

NIA used a naturally-sourced diet with varied protein sources; Wisconsin used a purified, limited-ingredient diet with substantially higher sucrose. The Wisconsin comparison is arguably CR-vs-metabolically-unhealthy-control rather than CR-vs-healthy-control.

Wisconsin restricted adults; NIA included both juvenile-onset and old-onset animals. The 2017 joint analysis found benefit in adult/old onset but not juvenile onset - so mixing them dilutes the effect.
Wisconsin used Indian-origin rhesus only; NIA included both Indian- and Chinese-origin animals. The Wisconsin cohort was also more homogeneous in age.

The Wisconsin 2009 primary analysis censored deaths judged 'not related to ageing'. Leonard Guarente publicly criticised this decision. Censoring on a post-randomisation, outcome-adjacent judgement is a live bias risk.

errors.study: Bannister et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2014 - 'Can people with type 2 diabetes live longer than those without?'
errors.claim_attacked: Diabetics on metformin monotherapy outlive matched non-diabetic controls, implying metformin is a geroprotector.
errors.flaw: Multiple, compounding: (a) SELECTION OF A SURVIVOR COHORT - remaining on metformin monotherapy for the study period selects patients whose diabetes never progressed, i.e. the healthiest and most treatment-responsive diabetics, while no analogous filter was applied to the non-diabetic comparator; (b) INFORMATIVE CENSORING - metformin initiators were censored at treatment intensification, an event caused by deteriorating health, so sicker person-time is removed from the exposed arm but not the control arm; (c) DISADVANTAGEOUS SELECTION INTO THE CONTROL GROUP - 'non-diabetic' primary-care controls include undiagnosed diabetics and people with less healthcare contact and therefore less risk-factor management; (d) HEALTHY-ADHERER effects; (e) the headline figures are UNADJUSTED mortality rates.
errors.existing_published_critique: A retrospective cohort re-analysis, 'Reassessing the evidence of a survival advantage in Type 2 diabetes treated with metformin compared with controls without diabetes', and a 2022 Danish cohort, both failed to replicate; the Danish data showed HIGHER mortality among metformin users than non-diabetics over long follow-up.
errors.correction: Re-run as an explicit TARGET TRIAL EMULATION: (1) define time zero as first metformin prescription for the exposed and a matched index date for controls; (2) use a NEW-USER, ACTIVE-COMPARATOR design (metformin vs sulphonylurea) rather than diabetic-vs-non-diabetic, which is not a treatment contrast at all; (3) analyse by INTENTION-TO-TREAT on the treatment strategy, and separately per-protocol with INVERSE-PROBABILITY-OF-CENSORING WEIGHTS so that censoring at intensification is de-confounded; (4) prespecify NEGATIVE CONTROL OUTCOMES (e.g. accidental death) - any apparent 'protection' against them quantifies residual healthy-user confounding; (5) prespecify a NEGATIVE CONTROL EXPOSURE; (6) replicate across >=3 independent national databases with a common protocol before any claim is made. Falsifiable prediction: under a correct design, the metformin-vs-non-diabetic mortality advantage disappears entirely.

errors.study: The metformin observational literature broadly (dementia, cancer)
errors.claim_attacked: Metformin reduces dementia and cancer incidence.
errors.flaw: IMMORTAL TIME BIAS. Patients must survive long enough to accumulate the exposure that defines them as 'users'; that guaranteed-survival time is misallocated to the exposed group. Time-window bias and time-lag bias operate in the same direction. Dai et al. (2022) found 8 of 13 (61.5%) metformin-dementia cohort studies contained immortal time bias or failed to address it, and concluded NONE clearly addressed all relevant time-related biases.
errors.existing_published_critique: Dai et al., J Alzheimers Dis Rep 2022 (systematic review of time-related biases); Suissa & Azoulay, Diabetes Care 2012, 'Metformin and the risk of cancer: time-related biases in observational studies'; a 2022 analysis showed metformin is NOT associated with colorectal cancer incidence when methods that avoid immortal time bias are used.
errors.correction: Align time zero with treatment initiation for every arm (no 'ever-user' definitions). Use LANDMARK ANALYSIS or time-varying exposure with correctly allocated person-time. In diabetes specifically, compare against an ACTIVE comparator initiated at the same disease stage to neutralise time-lag bias (metformin is first-line, so its comparators are by construction later-stage disease). Re-analysis prediction: effect sizes shrink toward the null, as they did for colorectal cancer.

errors.study: ITP astaxanthin, meclizine (GeroScience 2024) and mitoglitazone (GeroScience 2025) vs ITP GeroScience 2026
errors.claim_attacked: Astaxanthin (+12% male median, p=0.003), meclizine (+8%, p=0.03) and mitoglitazone (+9% male) are lifespan-extending compounds.
errors.flaw: NON-REPLICATION, and dose/schedule-specific effects reported as compound-level effects. The ITP's own 2026 report found that all three failed to extend lifespan when given at different doses or from later starting ages. Worse, in FEMALES, astaxanthin, late-start mitoglitazone and pioglitazone were each associated with SIGNIFICANTLY REDUCED lifespan when pooling all three sites. The original p-values (0.003, 0.03) were also not corrected for the number of agents tested within each cohort.
flaw_types: unreported harm in the non-responding sex
errors.existing_published_critique: The ITP's own 2026 GeroScience paper is the critique. It explicitly notes these compounds were 'previously associated with lifespan extension in the ITP' and showed no benefit at other doses or later start ages.
errors.correction: (1) Treat each dose x start-age x sex combination as a DISTINCT intervention and never claim a compound-level effect from one cell. (2) Require a prespecified same-dose, same-start-age REPLICATION cohort before a compound is described as positive - the ITP already does this for some agents (NDGA was replicated at three doses); make it universal. (3) Apply a false-discovery-rate correction across all agents within a cohort and report both raw and adjusted p. (4) MANDATORY SYMMETRIC HARM REPORTING: report the effect in the non-responding sex with the same prominence, including negative point estimates, in the abstract. (5) Public preregistration of the exact primary test before unblinding. Falsifiable prediction: applying FDR correction across each ITP cohort would demote several borderline male-only hits (p ~0.03-0.05) to null.

errors.study: The ITP positive-hit literature generally (acarbose, 17-alpha-estradiol, NDGA, canagliflozin, Protandim, aspirin, epicatechin, halofuginone, astaxanthin, meclizine)
errors.claim_attacked: These compounds 'extend lifespan' - stated without sex qualification in most secondary coverage and all consumer coverage.
errors.flaw: SINGLE-SEX RESULTS REPORTED AS GENERAL. Almost every ITP hit is male-specific or strongly male-biased. Acarbose: 22% male vs 5% female. 17-alpha-estradiol: males only, at every dose and start age. Canagliflozin: 14% male, zero female. The standard analysis runs SEPARATE log-rank tests per sex, which is not a test of whether the sexes differ - two tests, one significant and one not, is weak evidence of a sex difference.
flaw_types: absence of a formal interaction test
errors.existing_published_critique: The ITP itself repeatedly emphasises sex-specificity (e.g. 'four of the six positive interventions only worked in one sex'). The methodological point about separate-tests-vs-interaction-tests is standard but is not consistently applied in this literature.
errors.correction: Fit a single Cox model with a SEX x TREATMENT INTERACTION TERM and report the interaction hazard ratio with its CI and p-value as the primary evidence for sex-specificity. Power the cohorts for the INTERACTION, not for the main effect (detecting an interaction of a given size requires roughly 4x the N of detecting a main effect of that size) - this likely means the ITP is currently underpowered to establish most of its claimed sex differences, even though the sex differences are almost certainly real for the large ones like acarbose. Additionally, run gonadectomy sub-studies to test whether the male-specificity is hormonal or chromosomal; the 17-alpha-estradiol literature already has ovariectomy data to build on. Falsifiable prediction: for acarbose and canagliflozin the interaction test will be clearly significant; for meclizine and glycine it will not be.

errors.study: Strong et al., Aging Cell 2022 - captopril, male arm
errors.flaw: SHORT-LIVED CONTROL COHORT AT ONE SITE. The apparent male benefit was confounded by unusually low survival of the CONTROL animals at one of the three test sites. When the control curve is anomalously bad, any treatment looks good. This is exactly the failure mode that the ITP's three-site design exists to detect - and here it did detect it, but the result is still frequently cited as a positive.
errors.existing_published_critique: Acknowledged in the primary paper itself.
errors.correction: (1) Prespecify a CONTROL-QUALITY GATE: before unblinding treatment arms, compare each site's concurrent control survival against the pooled distribution of that site's historical controls; flag and prespecify handling (exclusion or down-weighting) for sites deviating beyond a stated threshold. (2) Report the SITE x TREATMENT interaction routinely. (3) Report a leave-one-site-out sensitivity analysis for every positive hit as a standard supplementary table. (4) Use a frailty (random-effects) Cox model with site as a random effect rather than simple pooling. Falsifiable prediction: captopril's male effect will not survive leave-one-site-out analysis.

errors.study: Strong et al., Aging Cell 2016 (metformin+rapamycin) and Strong et al., Aging Cell 2022 (rapamycin+acarbose)
errors.claim_attacked: Drug combinations are more potent than their components - e.g. 'a drug combo increases lifespan in mice by over 30%'.
errors.flaw: NON-CONCURRENT (HISTORICAL) CONTROL COMPARISON. The combination arms were compared to rapamycin-alone animals from PRIOR cohorts, not to concurrent single-agent arms. Cohort effects in mouse lifespan studies are large (diet lots, pathogen status, husbandry drift, technician effects). The ITP was appropriately candid about this for metformin+rapamycin - the combination's benefit over rapamycin-only HISTORICAL controls was NOT statistically significant - but the caveat is routinely dropped in secondary coverage.
flaw_types: loss of caveat in secondary reporting
errors.correction: Run a CONCURRENT FULL FACTORIAL: vehicle / drug A / drug B / A+B in the same cohort, at the same sites, powered for the INTERACTION contrast (A+B) - (A) - (B) + (vehicle), not merely for A+B vs vehicle. Report the interaction estimate with its CI. Where historical controls are unavoidable, model cohort as a random effect and report how much of the apparent gain is absorbed by it. Until a concurrent factorial is run, synergy claims for rapamycin+acarbose are UNSUPPORTED. Falsifiable prediction: a concurrent factorial will show additivity, not synergy, for metformin+rapamycin.

errors.study: ITP statistical methodology - reliance on the log-rank test
errors.claim_attacked: The ITP's list of negative compounds is a definitive list of things that do not affect ageing.
errors.flaw: TEST MISSPECIFICATION / LOW POWER AGAINST NON-PROPORTIONAL HAZARDS. The log-rank test is most powerful under proportional hazards and weights all failure times equally; it loses power when an intervention acts only early or only late in life. A Gehan-test reanalysis identified life-extending signals in metformin, enalapril, caffeic acid phenethyl ester, green tea extract and 17-DMAG that the log-rank test missed. A separate 'Temporal Efficacy Profiler' applied to 42 ITP compounds identified over TWICE as many compounds affecting survival, precisely because of sensitivity to time-varying efficacy.
flaw_types: post-hoc test-shopping risk in the other direction
errors.existing_published_critique: biorxiv 2024.02.17.579363 (Gehan test reanalysis); PMC11690145 (Temporal Efficacy Profiler).
errors.correction: Prespecify a TEST BATTERY rather than a single test, with multiplicity control: (1) DIFFERENCE IN RESTRICTED MEAN SURVIVAL TIME (RMST) at a prespecified horizon as the PRIMARY estimand - it is assumption-free, has a direct interpretation in days of life gained, and does not require proportional hazards; (2) log-rank and Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon as secondary, with the divergence between them reported as a diagnostic of non-proportional hazards; (3) Wang-Allison test for maximum lifespan; (4) a formal Grambsch-Therneau test of the proportional-hazards assumption reported for every compound. NOTE THE SYMMETRIC RISK: the Gehan/TEP reanalyses are themselves post-hoc test-shopping across 42 compounds and must be FDR-corrected; they generate hypotheses for re-testing, they do not resurrect metformin. Falsifiable prediction: prospectively re-testing metformin with RMST as the prespecified estimand will still be null.

errors.study: Colman et al., Science 2009 - Wisconsin rhesus caloric restriction
errors.claim_attacked: Caloric restriction extends life in primates.
errors.flaw: Two distinct problems. (a) OUTCOME-ADJACENT CENSORING: the primary analysis censored deaths adjudicated as 'not related to ageing'. That adjudication is post-randomisation, is not blinded to arm in any documented way, and is not independent of the outcome. Leonard Guarente publicly criticised this. (b) CONTROL-ARM CONFOUNDING: Wisconsin controls ate a purified, limited-ingredient diet with substantially higher sucrose than the NIA diet, plus ~20 g/day of extra chow available at will. The contrast is therefore closer to 'CR vs a metabolically adverse diet eaten to excess' than to 'CR vs healthy eating'. This is the same confound that makes rodent CR studies against obesogenic ad-libitum controls hard to interpret.
flaw_types: informative censoring on adjudicated cause of death
errors.existing_published_critique: Guarente's critique of the censoring decision; the 2017 Mattison et al. joint Nature Communications reconciliation documents the diet and feeding differences. The Wisconsin team's own 2014 Nature Communications paper reported all-cause (uncensored) mortality as also significant, which partially answers (a) but not (b).
errors.correction: (1) Make ALL-CAUSE mortality the primary endpoint always; report cause-specific analyses as secondary with blinded, independent, prespecified adjudication and publish the adjudication rubric and inter-rater reliability. (2) For (b): the definitive design is a 2x2 of diet quality x caloric level - i.e. CR and ad libitum arms on BOTH the purified/high-sucrose and the naturally-sourced diet - which separates 'eating less' from 'eating less of a bad diet'. This has never been run in primates and is the single most informative primate CR experiment still undone. (3) Measure and report per-animal ad libitum intake so the CR percentage is defined against a measured, not assumed, baseline.

errors.study: Mattison et al., Nature 2012 - NIA rhesus caloric restriction
errors.claim_attacked: Caloric restriction does NOT extend life in primates.
errors.flaw: NULL BY DESIGN. The NIA 'control' animals were PORTION-fed rather than truly ad libitum, ate less than the Wisconsin controls, and their lower intake was itself associated with better survival. A control arm that is partially calorie-restricted attenuates the treatment contrast toward zero. Compounded by (a) mixing juvenile-onset and old-onset animals, when the 2017 joint analysis concluded benefit occurs only with adult/old onset - so the juvenile stratum dilutes a real effect; and (b) mixing Indian- and Chinese-origin animals with differing lifespan distributions, inflating within-arm variance.
flaw_types: effect dilution by pooling non-responding strata
underpowered null reported as evidence of absence
errors.existing_published_critique: Colman (Wisconsin) publicly argued the NIA controls were themselves calorie-restricted; the 2017 Mattison et al. joint analysis formalised the age-at-onset finding.
errors.correction: (1) A null from a study with a contaminated control arm is NOT evidence of absence - report the minimum detectable effect and the CI on the survival difference, not just 'p>0.05'. (2) Define restriction against MEASURED per-animal ad libitum intake, re-measured periodically, not against a fixed portion. (3) PRESTRATIFY randomisation by genetic origin and by age at onset, and prespecify the adult-onset stratum as primary. (4) Pool individual-participant data from both studies and fit a single model with study, origin, onset-age and diet-type as covariates - a proper IPD meta-analysis rather than the narrative reconciliation that was published.

errors.study: CALERIE-2 (Waziry et al., Nature Aging 2023; Kraus et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2019)
errors.claim_attacked: A 25% caloric restriction slows human ageing by 2-3%, equivalent to a 10-15% mortality reduction.
errors.flaw: Three stacked problems. (a) TARGET-VS-ACHIEVED GAP: 25% CR was prescribed but only ~12-13% was achieved. The trial does not test the intervention it is named for; every citation of 'CALERIE tested 25% CR' is wrong. (b) SURROGATE-ENDPOINT SUBSTITUTION plus MULTIPLICITY: several DNA-methylation clocks were assessed and only DunedinPACE moved; PhenoAge and GrimAge did not. GrimAge is the clock best calibrated to mortality, so the most mortality-relevant measure was NULL. Reporting the one clock that moved is a selection over endpoints. (c) EXTRAPOLATION LAUNDERING: the '10-15% mortality reduction' figure is not a CALERIE result at all - it is imported from separate observational cohorts that calibrated DunedinPACE against mortality, and then applied to a trial-induced change. A drug-induced change in a biomarker need not carry the same prognostic meaning as a naturally-occurring difference in that biomarker. This is the classic surrogate-endpoint fallacy that killed CAST (antiarrhythmics), torcetrapib (HDL) and hormone replacement for CVD prevention.
flaw_types: extrapolation from observational calibration to interventional change
errors.existing_published_critique: The exploratory status of the cardiometabolic outcomes is declared in the Kraus et al. title itself. The bone loss is documented in Villareal et al., JBMR 2016 but is rarely co-reported with the DunedinPACE headline.
errors.correction: (1) Report the intervention by its ACHIEVED energy deficit, verified by doubly labelled water, and present a DOSE-RESPONSE analysis of achieved deficit vs DunedinPACE change - if CR is causal, that gradient must exist within the trial. Its absence would be strong evidence against. (2) PRESPECIFY ONE clock as primary; report all others with multiplicity adjustment. (3) Never convert a surrogate change into a mortality figure without stating it is an extrapolation with an unvalidated transfer assumption; better, state it as 'unknown'. (4) MANDATORY BALANCE SHEET: co-report the femoral neck and lumbar spine BMD losses and lean mass losses in the abstract alongside the DunedinPACE gain, since in an older population the fracture risk could plausibly exceed the ageing benefit. (5) The decisive study: long-term passive mortality follow-up of the CALERIE-2 cohort via registry linkage. It is cheap and it is the only thing that would convert this from surrogate to outcome evidence.

errors.study: Mannick et al., Sci Transl Med 2018 (RTB101 phase 2b) vs PROTECTOR-1 phase 3 (2019)
errors.claim_attacked: mTORC1 inhibition reduces infections and rejuvenates immune function in the elderly.
errors.flaw: NON-REPLICATION FROM PHASE 2b TO PHASE 3. The phase 2b reported reduced respiratory tract infections; the adequately powered phase 3 (n=1024, RTB101 10 mg daily for 16 weeks) found event proportions of 0.46 on drug vs 0.44 on placebo - numerically WORSE than placebo. Development was halted. The phase 2b signal was, in retrospect, consistent with a dose/population/endpoint selection that did not survive prespecification. The 2014 predecessor trial used an immunological SURROGATE (a ~20% improvement in vaccine antibody response), and the surrogate did not predict the clinical endpoint.
flaw_types: surrogate endpoint failed to predict clinical outcome
endpoint/subgroup selection in the earlier phase
errors.existing_published_critique: 'RTB101 and immune function in the elderly: Interpreting an unsuccessful clinical trial' (2020).
errors.correction: (1) Require that any phase 2 signal be replicated in an INDEPENDENT phase 2 with the identical prespecified primary endpoint, dose and population before phase 3 commitment. (2) Publish the phase 2b statistical analysis plan and the full set of endpoints and subgroups examined, so the selection space is visible. (3) Formally test surrogate validity: does the treatment effect on vaccine antibody titre mediate the treatment effect on infection? Run a mediation analysis; if the surrogate does not mediate, stop using it. (4) For geroscience specifically: this is the field's most instructive failure - an on-target, mechanistically coherent, biomarker-positive intervention that did nothing to the clinical endpoint at scale. It should be the default prior for every NAD+/senolytic/supplement biomarker result.

errors.claim_attacked: Low-dose rapamycin improves lean mass and well-being in ageing adults.
errors.flaw: PRIMARY ENDPOINT FAILED, SECONDARY SUBGROUP PROMOTED. Neither 5 mg nor 10 mg weekly reduced visceral adipose tissue (the prespecified primary outcome). The circulated positive finding - lean tissue mass +4.5% - is confined to WOMEN on the 10 mg dose only: a selection across sex x dose x outcome, in a trial of n=114 with no multiplicity control described. Compounding factors: the trial used COMPOUNDED rapamycin (variable pharmacokinetics, no verified blood levels reported in what was surfaced), was decentralised, and was conducted by a commercial telehealth provider that sells rapamycin - a direct industry-funding conflict.
flaw_types: primary endpoint failure with secondary promotion
subgroup selection (sex x dose x outcome)
industry funding / sponsor sells the product
errors.existing_published_critique: None located; the critique here is derived from the trial's own reported structure.
errors.correction: (1) Report the primary endpoint result in the abstract's first sentence and label all secondaries as hypothesis-generating. (2) Apply HIERARCHICAL (gatekeeping) TESTING: if the primary fails, no secondary may be declared significant. (3) Report the full endpoint inventory and the number of sex x dose x outcome comparisons performed, with FDR-adjusted p-values. (4) Measure and report TROUGH BLOOD RAPAMYCIN LEVELS - without exposure data an intermittent-dosing trial cannot distinguish 'the drug does not work' from 'the drug was not present'. (5) A replication must be independently funded and must prespecify lean mass in women on 10 mg as the single primary endpoint. Falsifiable prediction: an independently funded replication with that single prespecified endpoint will produce a substantially smaller effect than 4.5%.

errors.study: The alcohol J-curve literature (decades of cohort studies reporting moderate drinking as protective)
errors.claim_attacked: Moderate alcohol consumption reduces all-cause mortality.
errors.flaw: ABSTAINER BIAS / SICK-QUITTER BIAS. The 'non-drinker' reference group in most cohorts pools lifetime abstainers with FORMER drinkers, many of whom quit because they became ill (including from alcohol). This loads the reference category with high-risk people and manufactures an apparent benefit of moderate drinking. Secondary contributors: reference-group choice, cohort age at baseline, and failure to adjust for socioeconomic confounding (moderate drinking tracks with income and education in most Western cohorts). Zhao and Stockwell et al. showed that the apparent low-volume protective association becomes small and NON-SIGNIFICANT once these study characteristics are adjusted for.
errors.existing_published_critique: Zhao, Stockwell et al., JAMA Network Open 2023 (systematic review and meta-analysis); Stockwell et al., J Stud Alcohol Drugs 2024, 'Why do only some cohort studies find health benefits from low-volume alcohol use?'; Millwood et al., Lancet 2019 (Mendelian randomization, China Kadoorie Biobank, 512,715 participants, 161,498 genotyped for ALDH2-rs671 and ADH1B-rs1229984) found no protective effect of moderate intake on stroke and a causal hypertensive effect.
errors.correction: (1) Use LIFETIME ABSTAINERS ONLY as the reference and analyse former drinkers as a separate exposure category, never merged. (2) Apply a LANDMARK/LAG of >=5-10 years excluding baseline illness and early deaths to break reverse causation. (3) TRIANGULATE with Mendelian randomization using ALDH2-rs671 and ADH1B-rs1229984 - genotype is fixed at conception and cannot be caused by illness, so it is immune to sick-quitter bias. The MR estimates are monotonic, not J-shaped. (4) Where observational and MR estimates diverge, the divergence itself is the estimate of the bias. This case is the field's cleanest demonstration that a J-curve can be entirely an artefact of reference-group construction, and it should be the template for evaluating every other claimed J-curve (including the exercise U-curve).

errors.study: Mandsager et al., JAMA Network Open 2018 - cardiorespiratory fitness and mortality
errors.claim_attacked: Improving VO2max from low to elite cuts mortality risk five-fold (HR 5.04).
errors.flaw: This is the strongest OBSERVATIONAL association in the modifiable-risk literature, and it is routinely reported as if it were a causal effect of training. Three problems: (a) REVERSE CAUSATION - subclinical disease lowers treadmill performance before it kills, and fitness was measured ONCE, at a single point, in a population REFERRED for stress testing (i.e. clinically suspected of disease); (b) CONFOUNDING - fitness is a composite readout of genetics, cumulative activity, body composition, absence of subclinical disease, and socioeconomic position; the adjustment set cannot capture 'absence of subclinical disease'; (c) POPULATION SELECTION - a referred clinical cohort is not the general population, and the elite-fitness stratum in such a cohort is highly selected. No RCT has ever randomised humans to a VO2max level and measured mortality, and none can.
flaw_types: causal language applied to observational HR
errors.existing_published_critique: None specific located; the design limitations are acknowledged in general terms in the primary paper.
errors.correction: (1) LANDMARK ANALYSIS excluding all deaths in the first 2-5 years, which removes most reverse causation; report how much the HR attenuates - the attenuation is the bias estimate. (2) Use REPEATED fitness measurements and model CHANGE in fitness, which is far closer to the causal question ('if I train, do I benefit?') than level of fitness. (3) MENDELIAN RANDOMIZATION on genetically predicted cardiorespiratory fitness / handgrip strength to triangulate. (4) NEGATIVE CONTROL OUTCOMES insensitive to fitness. (5) State plainly that the causal effect of TRAINING is bounded by RCTs of exercise interventions, which produce far smaller VO2max changes than the gap between the low and elite strata - the observed HR of 5.04 spans a fitness range that no training programme can move a person across. The honest translation is: fitness is the best PREDICTOR, but the achievable causal effect of training is much smaller than the association implies.

errors.study: SELECT (Lincoff et al., NEJM 2023) as evidence that semaglutide is a geroprotector
errors.claim_attacked: GLP-1 receptor agonists slow ageing, evidenced by a 19% reduction in all-cause mortality.
errors.flaw: Four issues. (a) RELATIVE-VS-ABSOLUTE INFLATION: '20% MACE reduction' and '19% mortality reduction' are relative; the absolute risk reduction over ~40 months is small and the ARR/NNT were not reported prominently. (b) ENDPOINT HIERARCHY: all-cause mortality was not the protected primary endpoint; the HR 0.81 (0.71-0.93) sits below the primary MACE endpoint in the testing sequence. (c) POPULATION: enrolled patients had overweight/obesity AND established cardiovascular disease. Benefit in a high-risk secondary-prevention population says nothing about geroprotection in healthy people, and the effect is fully consistent with ordinary cardiometabolic risk-factor reduction (weight, blood pressure, lipids, inflammation) rather than modulation of ageing. (d) COVID CONFOUNDING: the trial ran through the pandemic peak; a JACC 2024 analysis found HR 0.84 (0.72-0.98) without COVID and 0.74 (0.55-0.99) with COVID, and cause-of-death classification was degraded during that period. Separately, the LEAN MASS cost (~40% of weight lost in the STEP-1 substudy) is a plausible long-term harm in older adults that no trial has powered against mortality.
flaw_types: surrogate mechanism attribution (geroprotection vs risk-factor reduction)
errors.existing_published_critique: The JACC 2024 SELECT mortality/COVID analysis; the SURMOUNT-1 and STEP-1 body-composition substudies.
errors.correction: (1) ALWAYS report ARR and NNT alongside the HR - retrieve the absolute event percentages and compute them (this agent could not; the figures were not surfaced). (2) To test geroprotection rather than risk-factor reduction, run the trial in a population WITHOUT established cardiovascular disease and WITHOUT obesity, with a composite of heterogeneous age-related endpoints (the TAME design logic). SURMOUNT-MMO is the closest existing test - retrieve its design and status. (3) MEDIATION ANALYSIS: what fraction of the mortality effect is mediated by weight, BP, LDL and hsCRP change? If mediation is near-complete, 'geroprotector' is the wrong word. (4) Prespecify DXA lean mass and grip strength as safety endpoints in every long GLP-1 trial in adults >65, and follow fracture and disability outcomes. (5) Adjudicate cause of death blinded and report a pandemic-period sensitivity analysis.

errors.study: The NAD+ precursor literature (NR and NMN)
errors.claim_attacked: NAD+ precursors restore youthful NAD+ levels and therefore combat ageing.
errors.flaw: MECHANISM-OUTCOME DISSOCIATION presented as evidence. Blood NAD+ rises reliably - it doubled in the MCI trial - and essentially nothing clinical follows. A meta-analysis of 8 NMN RCTs (n=342) found no benefit on fasting glucose, fasting insulin, HbA1c, insulin resistance or lipids. The NR MCI trial was null on cognition (primary), cerebral blood flow and blood pressure. And the ITP tested NICOTINAMIDE RIBOSIDE DIRECTLY IN MICE AND FOUND NO LIFESPAN EFFECT IN EITHER SEX - the cleanest possible refutation, and it is almost never cited in consumer material. The positive counter-evidence (Yi 2023, 6-minute walk test at 600/900 mg over 60 days) rests on a short, effort-sensitive functional surrogate. Additional structural problem: much of the positive NAD+ literature is produced or funded by entities selling the compounds.
flaw_types: selective citation ignoring the ITP null
errors.existing_published_critique: Prokopidis et al., J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2025 (muscle meta-analysis, effect estimates not retrieved); the NMN metabolic meta-analysis (PMC11557618); Harrison et al., Aging Cell 2021 (ITP NR null).
errors.correction: (1) Stop reporting blood NAD+ as an efficacy outcome; it is a pharmacodynamic confirmation of absorption, nothing more. Require demonstration of TISSUE NAD+ change in the target tissue and of downstream pathway flux (e.g. sirtuin or PARP activity), not just plasma concentration. (2) Prespecify hard or objective functional endpoints and durations >=12 months. (3) Effort-dependent endpoints such as the 6-minute walk test require rigorous double-blinding with an assessment of blinding integrity (ask participants to guess their allocation and report the result). (4) MANDATORY funding and conflict declaration in the abstract; run a meta-regression of effect size against sponsor type - the prediction is a clear sponsorship gradient. (5) Cite the ITP null for NR as the primary animal evidence, since it is the only multi-site, sex-stratified, genetically heterogeneous lifespan test of the compound that exists.

errors.study: The 'exercise U-curve' / 'too much exercise is bad' claim
errors.claim_attacked: There is a mortality ceiling or reversal at high exercise volumes.
errors.flaw: The claim conflates two different exposures with different evidence. For AEROBIC activity, Arem et al. found benefit continuing to 3-5x the recommended minimum (HR 0.61) with a PLATEAU, not a reversal. For CARDIORESPIRATORY FITNESS, Mandsager et al. explicitly found NO upper limit of benefit. The one place a J-curve genuinely appears in the retrieved evidence is MUSCLE-STRENGTHENING activity (Momma et al.), where benefit peaks at 30-60 min/week with no conclusive further benefit beyond ~60 min/week - and even there the finding is a plateau/attenuation in observational data, not demonstrated harm. Studies reporting harm at extreme volumes typically involve small numbers of very high-volume athletes, where selection and reverse causation dominate.
errors.existing_published_critique: The Arem and Mandsager findings are themselves the corrective.
errors.correction: (1) Report dose-response with SPLINES and confidence bands, and state explicitly whether the upper confidence band excludes the null at high doses - most 'U-curves' have bands that include no-harm. (2) Distinguish aerobic volume, aerobic intensity, resistance volume, and measured fitness as SEPARATE exposures; never pool. (3) Correct for exposure measurement error (self-reported activity is heavily misreported at the extremes) using validation substudies with accelerometry. (4) Apply landmark analysis to remove reverse causation. Falsifiable prediction: with device-measured activity and landmark analysis, the aerobic dose-response will be monotonically protective with a plateau and no reversal.

As an internal yardstick, in the Mandsager cohort smoking carried HR 1.41 (1.36-1.46), which UNDERSTATES lifetime smoking harm because it is a single-timepoint status in a referred cohort.

ranked_intervention_table.human_all_cause_mortality_effect: HR 5.04 (4.10-6.20) for low vs elite, i.e. ~0.20 protective
ranked_intervention_table.note: Strongest association of any modifiable factor measured, but observational only and the ACHIEVABLE causal effect of training is much smaller than the low-to-elite contrast. See errors.E14.
Pooled cohorts; CI not retrieved. Plateau, no reversal.
NOT VERIFIED IN THIS SESSION. High-quality RCT evidence exists and this almost certainly belongs in the top 5. Must be sourced. See coverage_gaps.

ranked_intervention_table.note: NOT VERIFIED IN THIS SESSION. Must be sourced (CTT collaboration meta-analyses). Note the ITP found atorvastatin+telmisartan did NOT extend mouse lifespan, which is expected and not contradictory - chow-fed mice do not develop human-like atherosclerosis.

ranked_intervention_table.evidence_grade: U for mortality; B for surrogates
ranked_intervention_table.note: DunedinPACE slowed 2-3%; PhenoAge and GrimAge unchanged. Documented harms: lumbar spine, total hip and femoral neck BMD loss; lean mass loss. In primates the evidence is genuinely contested (see rhesus_monkey_cr). Do not rank higher than 'unknown'.

ranked_intervention_table.evidence_grade: U in humans; A in mice
ranked_intervention_table.note: Best animal evidence in the field (up to +23% male / +26% female median in UM-HET3 at 42 ppm, replicated across doses, sites and start ages). In humans: the only adequately powered phase 3 of an mTOR inhibitor (RTB101) FAILED, and the only sizeable rapamycin RCT (PEARL) missed its primary endpoint. Known human harms of chronic dosing: immunosuppression, impaired glucose tolerance, dyslipidaemia, mouth ulcers/aphthous stomatitis, impaired wound healing; testicular degeneration and cataracts documented in mice. The gap between the mouse and human evidence is the single largest in geroscience.

ranked_intervention_table.human_all_cause_mortality_effect: UNKNOWN, and the observational evidence for benefit is unsound
ranked_intervention_table.evidence_grade: U (TAME not run); D and rejected for the observational claim
ranked_intervention_table.note: FAILED to extend lifespan alone in the ITP. The Bannister claim is biased (errors.E1). Konopka et al. showed metformin BLUNTS the VO2max and insulin-sensitivity gains from exercise training - i.e. it may antagonise the intervention ranked #2. On current evidence, prophylactic metformin in a healthy exercising adult has a plausible NET NEGATIVE expected value.

ranked_intervention_table.intervention: GLP-1 RAs as geroprotectors in healthy, non-obese people
ranked_intervention_table.note: No trial has tested this population. Do not extrapolate SELECT.

ranked_intervention_table.human_all_cause_mortality_effect: no evidence of any mortality effect; null on nearly all functional and metabolic endpoints
ranked_intervention_table.evidence_grade: B for the NULL on surrogates and function; U for mortality
ranked_intervention_table.note: NR failed outright in the ITP - no lifespan effect in either sex in mice. Blood NAD+ rises reliably and nothing follows. See errors.E16.
